title: Structural and dynamical behavior of methane-water systems under nanoconfinement
authors: José Torres-Arenas, Ángel M. Fernández-Fernández, Martín Pérez-Rodríguez, Manuel M. Piñeiro
abstract: We investigate the structural and dynamical behavior of methane water systems under nanoconfinement using molecular dynamics simulations across pore widths from 1 to 5 nm. Structural analysis reveals a strong and nonmonotonic dependence on confinement: while tetrahedral ordering partially recovers as confinement is reduced, cubic like order associated with clathrate precursors is maximized at intermediate pore sizes. Radial distribution functions show that three dimensional correlations are suppressed under strong confinement, whereas lateral ordering persists, indicating a reduction in the effective dimensionality of structural organization. Transport properties reflect the same structural competition. Parallel diffusion is nonmonotonic with pore size, while perpendicular motion is subdiffusive due to confinement induced trapping and heterogeneity. Methane exhibits stronger subdiffusion and remains dynamically coupled to the water matrix. A characteristic confinement length scale emerges at which structural ordering, dynamical heterogeneity, and solvent solute decoupling are simultaneously maximized. At strong confinement, three dimensional correlations are suppressed, leading to dimensional reduction, frustrated ordering, and inhibited nucleation.
summary: This work uses molecular dynamics simulations to map out how methane and water structure and move when squeezed into nanopores. The key finding is that structural organization doesn't simply increase or decrease with pore size; instead, a competition between local ordering and the inability to form full 3D structures defines critical length scales. This has implications for understanding gas hydrate stability in porous media.
main_problem: The study investigates how structural ordering and dynamic behavior of methane-water mixtures are altered when confined within nanopores.
main_result: Confinement leads to a non-monotonic competition between local structuring (maximizing at intermediate pores) and the suppression of extended 3D correlations, defining a characteristic length scale for maximum heterogeneity.
method: Molecular dynamics simulations were employed using all-atom force fields to track structural metrics and transport properties across varying pore widths.
model_or_system: The system models methane ($	ext{CH}_4$) and water ($	ext{H}_2	ext{O}$) confined within planar silica nanopores, simulating conditions relevant to hydrate formation.
key_observables: Radial distribution functions (RDFs), local order parameters ($F_{3}, F_{4}$), parallel and perpendicular diffusion coefficients ($D_{\parallel}, D_{\perp}$), and anomalous diffusion exponents ($\alpha$).
important_parameters: Pore widths ranging from 1 to 5 nm, temperatures between 250 K and 295 K.
main_assumptions: The simulation conditions are assumed to fall within the methane hydrate stability zone for the force field used.
figures_summary: Figures show density profiles of water/methane across pore sizes; RDFs illustrate local structure; plots detail non-monotonic changes in diffusion coefficients and anomalous exponents ($\alpha$) with pore size.
paper_structure: The paper systematically analyzes structural evolution (using order parameters and RDFs) followed by a detailed investigation of anisotropic transport properties, correlating dynamical decoupling ($\Delta\alpha$) directly to the observed structural frustration regimes.
why_interesting: While focused on liquid-state physics, the concept of confinement-induced dimensional reduction, frustrated ordering, and identifying critical length scales where multiple physical behaviors peak is highly relevant for understanding quantum confinement effects in nanoscale materials or engineered quantum systems.

Each panel shows the density variation along the confinement direction for two selected temperatures chosen to contrast regimes with and without pronounced structural ordering. In the 1 nm pore, where no three-dimensional ordering is observed at any temperature, the two most separated temperatures are shown. The profiles highlight the evolution of interfacial layering with pore size and temperature.

FIG. 2. Density profiles of methane across the pore for representative pore sizes (1, 3, and 5 nm). Each panel shows the density variation along the confinement direction for two selected temperatures chosen to contrast different structural regimes of the surrounding water. In the 1 nm pore, where no three-dimensional ordering is observed at any temperature, the two most separated temperatures are shown. The profiles illustrate how confinement-induced structuring of the host water affects methane interfacial localization and layering.
